# Draft:Battle of Cumae (215 BC)

Background
Little has survived of Polybius's account of Hannibal's army in Italy following the Battle of Cannae. Livy offers a more detailed narrative, though according to historian Adrian Goldsworthy, "his reliability is often suspect," particularly in his descriptions of battles. Despite these concerns, shared by many modern historians, Livy's work remains the most comprehensive surviving source for this phase of the war. After this battle, Hannibal soon achieved his first significant political and strategic gains. Several communities began to defect from Rome, including the Campani, Atellani, Calatini, parts of Apulia, the Samnites (except the Pentri), all of the Bruttians, the Lucanians, the Uzentini, and much of the Greek coastal cities, such as Tarentum, Metapontum, Croton, and Locri, as well as all the Cisalpine Gauls. Compsa and the Hirpini also went over to the Carthaginians. However, Neapolis resisted and remained loyal to Rome.
To consolidate these gains, Hannibal sent his brother Mago south into Bruttium with a portion of the army to accept the surrender of defecting cities and subdue those that resisted. Meanwhile, Hannibal advanced into Campania. After a series of negotiations, he secured the defection of Capua, then considered the second most important city in Italy after Rome.
